info.desc: Nevermind is the second studio album by the American grunge band Nirvana, released on September 24, 1991. Produced by Butch Vig, Nevermind was the group's first release on Geffen Records, which signaled its move away from Seattle-based independent record label Sub Pop. Front man Kurt Cobain sought to make music outside of the restrictive confines of the Seattle grunge scene, drawing influence from groups such as the Pixies and its use of loud/quiet song dynamics. Nevermind was a surprise success by late 1991, largely due to the success of its lead single "Smells Like Teen Spirit". By January 1992 it .

podcast.body: "Nevermind" was a pivotal album that exploded everything that had been building in indie and alternative music throughout the 1980s. It refined the sound pioneered by bands like Husker Dew and Sonic Youth, incorporating influences from Kiss, Black Sabbath, and The Beatles. It was one of the first alternative records to achieve success on both radio and MTV, establishing Nirvana as a bridge between the underground and mainstream rock scenes. "Everything that had been building through the 1980s, as far as indie and alternative and underground was concerned, exploded with this record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Although "Smells Like Teen Spirit" became the album's unexpected hit single, the record label originally intended "Lithium" to be the first single. "Teen Spirit" was considered a "trial balloon" and was not expected to be a hit. "The real first single from Nevermind was going to be lithium."

podcast.body: Considered the most famous of the "Holy Trinity of Grunge" albums, its single was released on August 27, 1991, with the full album following on September 24, 1991. Within weeks, it was selling 300,000 copies a week and, by January, dethroned Michael Jackson's "Bad" from the number one spot on the Billboard charts, driving the rise of grunge and making alternative music mainstream. "Nirvana's never mind is the most famous of the Holy Trinity of Grunge albums."

podcast.body: Depending on the specific edition or pressing of the album "Nevermind" one possesses, a hidden track is likely present in the silence following the song "Something in the Way". This audio piece would roar into the listener's ears ten minutes after the preceding song concluded, often surprising millions who believed the album had finished. "It roars into your ears ten minutes after something in the way ends. And it scared the crap out of millions of people who thought they had let Nevermind run out."

This highlights the period before the grunge explosion, showing that many key bands of the movement were still in their formative or pre-breakthrough stages. "Nirvana still hadn't gotten into the studio to record Nevermind."

The immense and unexpected success of Nevermind, highlighted by the new SoundScan system, prompted record labels to drastically shift their focus, initiating what became known as the "Grunge Gold Rush." "Nirvana's never-mind album was certified to selling 300,000 copies a week, every week, for months."

podcast.body: Nirvana's 1991 major label debut, *Nevermind*, was initially expected by Atlantic Records to sell only as well as the last Sonic Youth album. However, it achieved an astounding commercial success, ultimately selling 10 million copies and shattering all expectations, becoming a pivotal album in the grunge movement. "an oft repeated story about Nirvana was that their 1991 major label debut Nevermind was only expected to sell as well as the last Sonic Youth album, a benchmark that came to seem absurd when Nevermind sold 10 million copies."

podcast.body: Nirvana's album "Never Mind" was released after they signed with DGC Records, a decision influenced by Sonic Youth's earlier signing with the same label. Kurt Cobain, a huge Sonic Youth fan, believed that if they could maintain creative control on a major label, Nirvana could too. "Nirvana signed, released Never Mind, Restless History."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Nirvana's second album and major label debut, produced by Butch Vig for DGC Records. Despite initial sales projections of 100,000 copies, it debuted at number 144 on the Billboard 200 and surged to number one after Christmas 1991, displacing Michael Jackson. The album, featuring a naked baby chasing a dollar bill on its cover, blended Seattle punk and metal with "enticing hooks" and a "pop sensibility." "The album with a naked baby on the cover, chasing a dollar bill on a fishing line, with song titles like Lithium, Territorial Pissings, and Stay Away was now the number one album in the country."

podcast.body: Released in 1991, "Nevermind" is considered one of the great albums of the 1990s. During its creation, Kurt Cobain expressed concerns about potential plagiarism, worrying that parts of "Smells Like Teen Spirit" resembled Boston's "More Than a Feeling" and that the quiet/loud structure mirrored The Pixies. The album's momentum was also potentially threatened by a copyright controversy surrounding the second single, "Come As You Are." "One of the great, great albums of the 1990s was Never Mind by Nirvana."

podcast.body: Released on September 24, 1991, less than a month after Pearl Jam's "Ten," this album became the second part of the "Holy Trinity of Records" that launched grunge into the mainstream. Initial expectations were low, with only 46,251 copies manufactured and shipped. However, due to the overwhelming public reaction to its first single, the album sold out instantly and was moving 300,000 copies weekly within eight weeks, mobilizing a vast market of Generation X listeners. "Within eight weeks, this record was selling 300,000 copies every seven days."

podcast.body: Released on September 24th, 1991, initial shipments totaled 46,251 copies, with industry expectations of only 50,000 sales if lucky. This album arrived during a stagnant period for rock music, dominated by classic rock, unamusing hair metal power ballads, and "crappy phony pop stars." It resonated deeply with Generation Xers who were seeking an emotional voice amidst recession and the Gulf War, providing them with music that spoke to their anger and fear. *Nevermind* swiftly became a monumental success, changing the entire rock landscape and shifting alternative music into the mainstream. "Never mind was one of those records that changed everything."

podcast.body: The album's release on September 24, 1991, drastically altered the musical landscape, marking a pivotal moment in the speaker's musical life. It shared its release date with *Blood Sugar Sex Magik* by the Red Hot Chili Peppers. Warner (GDGC's) initially projected sales of 50,000 to 100,000 copies, but the album quickly soared to 300,000 copies per week. In January, it famously dislodged Michael Jackson from the number one spot on the Billboard album charts. "I remember September 25, 1991 walking into Medeville High School and my entire musical landscape changed because of what happened the day before with the drop of Nevermind."

podcast.body: This album became "the biggest thing in the world" after its release. In the spring of 1992, following its massive success, Kurt Cobain sought to rewrite the band's royalty arrangements, demanding 90% of songwriting royalties, backdated to the album's September 1991 release. After heated arguments, Kurt was eventually "bargained down to 75%." "In the spring of 1992, after the Never Mind album had become the biggest thing in the world, Kurt Cobain decided he wanted to rewrite the band's royalty arrangements."

The follow-up, *In Utero*, was intentionally made to contrast with its polished sound. "Kurt also didn't like the record company game very much. He thought that never mind was too slick and wasn't punk rock enough."

podcast.body: This album had a "sharp sheen" applied to it by mastering engineer Andy Wallace, who extended the high frequencies of the two-track mix provided by the band and producer Butch Vig. This mastering technique helped the songs achieve greater clarity and cut-through, especially when compared to the original studio mix, which sounded muffled and dull. "Andy Wallace applied the sharp sheen to Nirvana's Nevermind album."

The band initially hoped to sell around 200,000 copies, but "Nevermind" became an unprecedented success, selling 300,000 copies a week by Christmas. It sold its first million copies in just 65 days and doubled that figure in another 41 days, ultimately staying on the Billboard charts for 92 uninterrupted weeks and generating over $100 million in gross revenues.
